title: 👑 Elite Challenge: Choosing the Right Function

options.text: Would you mind to carry this bag for me?
Could you carry this bag for me, please?
Can I help you with this bag?
Do you need any help with this bag?

questions.explanation: The error is in "Would you mind to carry this bag for me?": after "mind" the verb takes -ing — Would you mind carrying this bag for me? The other three are correct: "Could you" + bare verb is a request, and "Can I help you…?" / "Do you need any help…?" are offers.

questions.prompt: Your neighbour, an old man, is carrying heavy shopping bags up the stairs. What do you say to him?

options.text: Can you help me with the bags?
Could you carry my bags, please?
Do you need any help, sir?
Would you mind carrying the bags?

questions.explanation: You want to help him, so you OFFER help, and you are the helper: Do you need any help, sir? The three other sentences ask HIM to do something for you — requests to an old man who is already carrying too much. "Can you help me" is the classic swap with "Can I help you".

questions.prompt: You meet your cousin by chance at the airport. What do you say?

options.text: How nice to see you here!
What a pity to see you here!
How a surprise to see you here!
What nice to see you here!

questions.explanation: "How nice to" + verb is the exclamation of a happy surprise: How nice to see you here! "What a pity" expresses disappointment, which is wrong for a happy meeting; "How a surprise" and "What nice" mix the two patterns — What a + noun, How + adjective.

options.text: I hope you to pass your exam.
I hope that you pass your exam.
I hope passing your exam.
I hope that you passing your exam.

questions.explanation: "I hope that" is followed by a full clause, subject + verb: I hope that you pass your exam. "I hope you to pass" copies "I want you to pass" — a common mistake; "I hope passing" has no subject, and "that you passing" has no real verb.

questions.prompt: Your friend asks: "Cinema or TV tonight?" You don't prefer one or the other. Which answer shows this?

options.text: I'm interested in the cinema.
It sounds interesting.
I don't mind.
I'd like to know more about it.

questions.explanation: "I don't mind" shows indifference: either choice is fine for you. "I'm interested in the cinema" chooses the cinema; "It sounds interesting" and "I'd like to know more about it" show interest, not indifference.

questions.prompt: In a shop, the assistant shows you a blue skirt — exactly the one you were looking for. What do you say?

options.text: I don't care what colour the skirt is.
What a pity! This is the skirt.
It sounds interesting, this skirt.
This is just what I was looking for.

questions.explanation: "This is just what I wanted / needed / was looking for" expresses satisfaction. "I don't care…" shows indifference, "What a pity!" shows disappointment, and "It sounds interesting" shows interest in something you hear about — none of them says the skirt is exactly right.
